title: Drinking on a Boat: BUI Limits, Safety Rules and Booze Cruise Tips
excerpt: At what alcohol level is a boater impaired? The 0.08 BUI limit, whether passengers can drink, why alcohol hits harder on the water, and how to survive a booze cruise safely.
metaDescription: At what alcohol level is a boater impaired? The 0.08 BUI limit, passenger rules, why alcohol hits harder on water, and booze cruise safety tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** in the United States, a boat operator is legally impaired at a blood or breath alcohol concentration of **0.08% or higher**, the same number used for driving a car. That is the federal standard for recreational boats, and nearly every state uses it too. Operators of commercial vessels face a stricter federal limit of **0.04%**. You can also be charged below those numbers if an officer believes alcohol has impaired your ability to run the boat safely. Passengers are a different story, and the rules for them vary by state. This guide explains the limits, why alcohol hits harder on the water, how to enjoy a drink on a boat or a booze cruise without it going wrong, and the warning signs that mean someone needs help right away.

**The quick rules:** The person at the helm should not drink. Everyone else should pace themselves, eat, drink water between drinks, and stay out of the water once they've had more than a drink or two. Wear or keep a life jacket within reach, especially after dark. Don't mix alcohol with seasickness medicine without reading the label first, because most of those pills and patches warn against it.

> **This is not legal or medical advice.** Boating laws differ by state and country, and this article gives general guidance only. Check your state's boating agency for the exact rules where you'll be on the water. **Call 911 (or radio the Coast Guard on VHF channel 16) right away if** someone on board is confused and can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has pale or bluish skin, has gone into the water and is struggling, or has hit their head. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning, a head injury, or drowning, and they are emergencies.

## At What Breath Alcohol Level Would a Boater Be Considered Impaired?

This is the question most people are searching for, often because it shows up on a boating safety course or exam. Here is the straight answer.

- **Recreational boats (federal standard):** a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of **0.08% or more**. Federal regulations (33 CFR Part 95) set this limit for recreational vessels on waters where the state hasn't set its own standard. In practice, almost every state has adopted 0.08% as its own boating limit.
- **Commercial vessels:** **0.04% or more** under the same federal rules. That covers people operating boats for hire, which includes the crew of a charter boat or a party cruise.
- **Under 21:** many states apply a much lower limit, sometimes close to zero, to young operators. Check your state's rules.
- **Below the limit:** you can still be charged with boating under the influence (BUI) if your behavior or performance shows you're impaired, even if your number is under 0.08%.

Breath and blood readings are treated as equivalent for these limits. A breath test measures the alcohol in the air from deep in your lungs, and the device converts that into an estimate of what's in your blood. So if a boating course asks "at what breath alcohol level would a boater be considered intoxicated," the expected answer in most US states is 0.08.

### How many drinks gets you to 0.08?

There's no reliable drink count, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. Your BAC depends on your body weight, sex, how fast you drink, whether you've eaten, how strong the drinks are, and your own metabolism. A smaller person drinking canned cocktails in the sun on an empty stomach can get there surprisingly fast. A heavy pour in a plastic cup can easily be two standard drinks.

Your body clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, and nothing you do speeds that up. Coffee, cold water, and a swim don't lower your BAC. Our guide on [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) explains the math and why "I feel fine" is a poor test.

## Is It Legal to Drink on a Boat?

Usually, yes, for passengers, with some important limits. Unlike cars, most US states don't have a blanket open-container ban on boats, so passengers of legal drinking age can often drink while the boat is underway. But the details vary a lot:

- **The operator is the key.** Every state prohibits operating a boat while impaired. Some states also bar the operator from drinking at all while the boat is moving, regardless of BAC.
- **Some waters ban alcohol outright.** Certain lakes, state parks, beaches, sandbars, and local waterways ban alcohol or glass containers. Federal lands and some marinas have their own rules.
- **Implied consent.** Many states have implied-consent laws for boating. By operating a boat, you agree to a breath or blood test if an officer has reason to think you're impaired, and refusing can carry its own penalty.
- **Underage drinking is illegal on a boat just as it is on land.** The boat owner or the adult who supplied the alcohol may face consequences too.

If you're renting a boat or visiting another state, look up the local rules before you go. A five-minute check of the state boating or wildlife agency's website will tell you what applies.

## What Happens If You Get a BUI?

A boating under the influence charge is a criminal offense in every state, not a minor ticket. Depending on where you are and whether anyone was hurt, penalties can include:

- Fines and court costs
- Jail time, especially for repeat offenses or if someone is injured or killed
- Loss of your boating privileges, and in some states, suspension of your **driver's license** as well
- Required boating safety or substance-use courses
- Having your boat impounded

Enforcement is real. The US Coast Guard can stop and board boats for safety and documentation checks, and state marine patrols often have similar powers, so you can be checked without having done anything visibly wrong. Each summer, a national campaign called **Operation Dry Water**, run by state boating agencies with the Coast Guard, steps up BUI patrols around the Fourth of July weekend.

## Why Alcohol Hits Harder on the Water

People often say they "feel it more" on a boat, and that's not just in their heads. The Coast Guard and boating safety groups have long warned that the conditions on a boat amplify the effects of alcohol. Several things stack up at once.

### Sun, wind, heat, and motion wear you down

Hours of sun glare, wind, engine noise and vibration, and the constant rocking of the boat cause a kind of fatigue sometimes called "boater's fatigue" or "boater's hypnosis." It slows your reaction time and makes you tired on its own. Add alcohol and the two effects compound, so a drink or two can leave you foggier than the same amount at a backyard barbecue.

### Dehydration sneaks up on you

Alcohol makes you pee more because it suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. On a hot day you're also losing water through sweat, often without noticing because the breeze keeps you feeling cool. Dehydration adds to the headache, fatigue, and dizziness, and sets you up for a rough next morning. Our guide to [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains the mechanism in more detail.

### Your balance is already being tested

Alcohol affects the inner ear, which is your body's balance sensor, and it slows the signals between your eyes, brain, and muscles. On land, that might mean a little wobble. On a moving deck, it means slipping, falling against hard edges, or going overboard. Many boating falls happen at the worst moments: standing to pee off the side, moving around while the boat is moving, or climbing back aboard from the water.

### Your judgment about the water slips

Alcohol makes people more confident and less careful. That's the part that turns a fun day into an emergency: deciding to swim to shore, jumping off a moving boat, skipping the life jacket, or letting someone who has been drinking drive the boat back. The Coast Guard's annual recreational boating statistics have consistently listed alcohol as a leading known contributing factor in fatal boating accidents.

## Swimming After Drinking: The Biggest Real Risk

If you remember one thing from this article, make it this: **the riskiest moment on a boating day is often not the drinking, it's getting in the water afterward.**

Alcohol makes drowning more likely in several ways at once. It weakens your coordination and swimming ability. It makes you misjudge distance and current. It can make you feel warmer than you are, while your body is actually losing heat faster. And sudden immersion in cold water triggers a gasp reflex (cold shock) that can cause you to inhale water, which is much harder to manage when you're impaired.

Safer habits for a boat day:

- **Set a rule before you leave the dock:** nobody swims after a certain number of drinks, and nobody swims alone.
- **Wear a life jacket in the water,** even if you're a strong swimmer. Coast Guard data has shown for years that most people who drown in boating accidents weren't wearing one.
- **Turn off the engine** and make sure the propeller is stopped before anyone gets in or out of the water near the stern.
- **No diving** into water you can't see the bottom of. Shallow sandbars cause serious neck and spine injuries.
- **Keep someone sober watching the swimmers.** A person in trouble in the water often doesn't splash or shout. They may just quietly slip under.
- **No swimming after dark** if anyone has been drinking.

## How to Enjoy a Drink on a Boat Safely

None of this means you can't have a beer on a sunny afternoon. It means planning a little more than you would on land.

1. **Pick a sober skipper.** Treat the boat operator exactly like a designated driver. They should have zero drinks, not "just a couple," because they're responsible for everyone on board, and conditions can change fast.
2. **Eat before and during.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Pack real snacks, not just chips: sandwiches, wraps, fruit, nuts, cheese.
3. **Alternate every drink with water.** Bring more water than you think you need. A good habit is a full bottle of water between each alcoholic drink.
4. **Choose lower-strength drinks.** Light beer, wine spritzers, and lower-alcohol seltzers go further than strong mixed drinks or shots. Check the label on canned cocktails, since some are much stronger than a beer.
5. **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour. Our guide on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk) has more practical pacing tips.
6. **Use cans and plastic, not glass.** Broken glass on a wet deck or on a beach is a real injury risk, and many waterways ban it anyway.
7. **Protect yourself from the sun.** Sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses, and shade breaks. Sunburn and heat exhaustion make everything worse, and people who are drinking tend to forget to reapply sunscreen.
8. **Keep life jackets accessible,** and make sure kids and weak swimmers wear theirs the whole time.
9. **Plan the ride home.** The trip from the marina to home is a car trip. Whoever drives needs to be sober too. Our guide on [how long to wait after drinking before you drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) covers this.

Much of this overlaps with general advice for a long afternoon of drinking outdoors. Our [day drinking guide](/never-hungover/day-drinking) goes into more detail on pacing a full day.

## Booze Cruise Survival Guide

A booze cruise or party boat is a little different from a day on a friend's boat. You're not the operator, the crew handles safety, and the whole point is the party. That makes it easier to relax, but also easier to overdo it, especially with an open bar, music, and a few hours to fill.

### Before you board

- **Eat a proper meal** with some protein and fat an hour or two beforehand. Boarding hungry is the most common mistake.
- **Hydrate during the day** so you don't start the cruise already behind.
- **Check the seasickness situation.** If you're prone to motion sickness, think about this in advance (see the medication section below).
- **Know how you're getting home.** Arrange a ride, taxi, or rideshare before you board, so you're not making that decision after the cruise.

### On board

- **Start slow.** The first hour of an open bar is when people drink fastest. Open with a water or a lighter drink.
- **Count your drinks honestly.** Free-pour cocktails on party boats are often stronger than a standard drink.
- **Stay off the rails and edges.** Don't sit on the railing or lean over the side, and move carefully on wet or crowded decks.
- **Stick with your group** and agree to check on each other. If someone disappears, look for them right away.
- **Stay in the shade when you can,** and keep water in hand on day cruises.
- **Listen to the crew.** On commercial vessels, crew members are trained for emergencies, and federal rules hold them to a stricter alcohol limit for exactly that reason.

### After you dock

Drink a big glass of water, eat something before bed, and leave the car. The motion can stay with you for a while after you step off (a lingering rocking feeling sometimes called "sea legs" or "dock rock"), and alcohol can make that wobble feel worse. If you're working on a hangover the next day, our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps an upset stomach.

## Seasickness Medicine and Alcohol: Read the Label

This is the part a lot of people miss. The most common over-the-counter motion-sickness pills, such as **dimenhydrinate** (Dramamine Original) and **meclizine** (sold as Dramamine Less Drowsy and Bonine), are antihistamines. They work partly by making you drowsy, and alcohol is a sedative too. Together they can make you much sleepier, slower, and more uncoordinated than either one alone. Their labels warn against drinking alcohol while taking them.

The prescription **scopolamine** patch also carries warnings about alcohol and about drowsiness, confusion, and blurred vision. Some people also find that alcohol itself makes motion sickness worse.

If you get seasick easily and plan to drink, talk to a pharmacist or doctor before the trip. They can help you choose an option and understand how much caution you'd need with alcohol. Non-drug strategies help too: stay in the middle of the boat where motion is lowest, keep your eyes on the horizon, get fresh air, and avoid reading or looking at your phone.

## When Someone on Board Needs Help

Being on the water makes emergencies more dangerous because help is further away. Know the signs and act early. **Call 911 on a cell phone or use VHF radio channel 16 to reach the Coast Guard** if someone:

- Can't be woken up or is very hard to wake
- Is confused, disoriented, or can't stand
- Is vomiting while drowsy or passed out (turn them on their side so they don't choke)
- Has slow or irregular breathing, or long gaps between breaths
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin
- Has a seizure
- Has hit their head, especially if they've been drinking
- Went into the water and was underwater, coughed up water, or is struggling to breathe afterward, even if they seem okay at first

Don't let someone who seems very drunk "sleep it off" alone, and never leave them alone near the edge of the boat. Our guide to [the signs of alcohol poisoning](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to watch for and what to do while you wait for help.

Signs of heat illness matter too: heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea, and cramps suggest heat exhaustion, and someone who stops sweating, becomes confused, or has hot, dry skin may have heatstroke, which is an emergency. Get them into shade, cool them with water, and call for help.

## The Next Morning: Why Boat Days Hurt

A long day of sun and drinks often leads to a worse hangover than the same number of drinks indoors. Dehydration from heat and sweat, too little food, sun exposure, poor sleep, and lingering motion all pile on. A few things that help:

- **Rehydrate** with water and something that has electrolytes. Our guide on [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains what's worth using.
- **Eat** something bland and filling once your stomach allows.
- **Treat sunburn** with cool showers and moisturizer, and stay out of the sun.
- **Rest.** There's no shortcut. Time is what actually clears a hangover.

For more on handling summer heat and alcohol together, see our [summer alcohol safety guide](/never-hungover/summer-alcohol-consumption-dhm-safety-guide), and for the habits with the best evidence for an easier morning, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

Some people who drink at boat parties, weddings, and summer events like to bring a DHM supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people find it helps them feel better the next morning, but there's no good evidence that it lowers your BAC, keeps you sober, or makes it safe to drive a boat or swim after drinking. It doesn't change anything in this article about the 0.08 limit or water safety.

If you'd like to try it, a popular choice is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a lower-cost single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- In the US, a recreational boater is considered legally impaired at a BAC or breath alcohol level of **0.08% or higher**, and commercial operators at **0.04%**. You can be charged below those levels if you're visibly impaired.
- Passengers can often drink legally, but rules vary by state and waterway, so check before you go.
- Sun, wind, heat, and motion make alcohol hit harder on a boat.
- The skipper should not drink. Treat them like a designated driver.
- The biggest danger is swimming after drinking. Wear life jackets and keep someone sober watching the water.
- Don't combine seasickness medication with alcohol without checking the label and asking a pharmacist.
- Know the signs of alcohol poisoning and heat illness, and call for help early. Help is further away on the water.

Planning a bigger trip on the water? Our guide to [drinking on a cruise](/never-hungover/drinking-on-a-cruise) covers multi-day sailing, drink packages, and seasickness medicine.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**At what breath alcohol level would a boater be considered impaired?**

In most of the United States, 0.08% or higher, the same as for driving a car. That's the federal standard for recreational boats, and nearly every state uses it. Commercial vessel operators face a stricter federal limit of 0.04%, and some states set a lower limit for operators under 21. You can still be charged with boating under the influence below these levels if an officer sees signs of impairment.

**Can passengers drink alcohol on a boat?**

In many US states, yes, as long as they're of legal drinking age, because most states don't apply car-style open-container laws to boats. But some lakes, parks, sandbars, and local waterways ban alcohol or glass, and rules vary by state. The operator must stay under the legal limit, and some states don't allow the operator to drink at all while underway. Check the local rules before you go.

**Is a BUI as serious as a DUI?**

It's treated as a criminal offense in every state, and penalties can include fines, jail time, loss of boating privileges, boat impoundment, and in some states suspension of your driver's license. Penalties get much heavier if someone is injured or killed. Many states also have implied-consent laws, so refusing a breath or blood test can bring its own penalty.

**Why do I feel drunker on a boat?**

Several things on the water add to alcohol's effects. Sun, heat, wind, engine noise, vibration, and the constant motion of the boat cause fatigue that slows your reactions even without alcohol. You also tend to get dehydrated faster in the heat, and the moving deck puts extra demands on your balance. Together, these can make the same number of drinks feel stronger than they would on land.

**Is it safe to swim after drinking on a boat?**

It's one of the riskiest things you can do on a boating day. Alcohol weakens coordination, makes you misjudge distance and currents, and makes it harder to handle cold-water shock. If you swim at all after drinking, keep it to a minimum, wear a life jacket, make sure the engine is off, never swim alone or after dark, and have a sober person watching. The safest choice is to stay out of the water once you've had more than a drink or two.

**Can I take Dramamine if I'm drinking on a boat?**

The common motion-sickness pills dimenhydrinate (Dramamine Original) and meclizine (Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy) are antihistamines that cause drowsiness, and their labels warn against drinking alcohol while taking them. The combination can make you much sleepier and less coordinated, which is dangerous on a boat. Talk to a pharmacist or doctor before your trip if you get seasick and plan to drink.

**How do you survive a booze cruise?**

Eat a solid meal before boarding, start slowly once the bar opens, and alternate each drink with water. Count your drinks honestly, since free-pour cocktails are often stronger than standard drinks. Stay away from the rails, stick with your group, and plan your ride home before you board so nobody drives afterward.

**Does DHM keep you sober enough to drive a boat?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol level or reduces impairment, and it does nothing to make operating a boat or swimming safer after drinking. Some people take it to feel better the next morning, but the operator should still have zero drinks, and the legal limits apply no matter what supplement you take.
